Expressing Necessity
You use a variety of modals to express necessity or obligation. Let's compare some of the most common ones:
Must vs. Have to
Must is stronger and more direct than have to. Must implies that the action is absolutely necessary. You use have to in less formal writing and in speaking.
You can use have to in all tenses to talk about the past, present and future, whereas must is only used to talk about the present.

They must prepare a report.
They have to prepare a report.
They had to prepare a report.
They will have to prepare a report.
Must vs. Should

You use must to talk about necessity in the present.
She must obey the rules.

You use should to give strong strong advice. You can use should instead of must when you want to be less direct in how you sound to others.
Compare:

You must do it today. (strong necessity, obligation)
You should do it today. (advice, recommendation)
Have got to vs. Have to / Need

You use have got to in more casual conversations. It is less formal than have to and need.
You usually refer to a noun after the verb need (I need help).
We don't have to do this debriefing session right now, Amy.
You need to pace yourself.
Alright, but we don't need to go into too much detail.
I really must get the photos printed up so I can show you.
We will have to do our part, of course.
Adverb Clauses of Condition and Purpose
You use adverb clauses introduced with conjunctions to explain the purpose of or to add a condition to an action.
Adverb clauses can put a condition on an action. You use the conjunctions if, whether, provided that and unless to introduce the condition.
Adverb clauses can explain the reason or purpose of an action. You use the conjunctions that, so that, in order that and lest to introduce the clause.
Look at the chart for a summary of these two types of adverb clause and the conjunctions that introduce them.

Candice: We don't have to do this debriefing session right now, Amy. You just got back for crying out loud! You need to pace yourself.
Amy: I know, but I really want to do it right away so that I don't forget anything.
Candice: Alright, but we don't need to go into too much detail. I'll just get you to print up a full progress report next week, when you're less exhausted. So, what were your impressions?

Amy: What a life-altering experience! It's been a real eye-opener. I really must get the photos printed up so I can show you. It's an impoverished country, to be sure. The AIDS pandemic has really devastated the local community. Yet the orphans are so grateful for everything they have.
Candice: I know, it's so sad. It really helps us to stay motivated in our fundraising efforts here at home. So how much progress has been made on the medical center?
Amy: It will be finished on time provided that local conditions cooperate. I'll have Samuel send you the updated budget.
Candice: Well, unless there's some unforeseen disaster, I expect it will be done within the next year, which is fantastic.

Amy: Right. We will have to do our part, of course. We must continue to host benefits and crowdfunding campaigns so that the initiatives continue to be well-funded.
Candice: If they continue to do their part in Lesotho, we will continue to do our part here at home. That's our commitment to them. Is there anything else?
Amy: Just some minor details. One of the buildings at the foster home will have to be repaired, and Samuel will need to get ...
Candice: We can have that kind of stuff taken care of next week. Now take the afternoon off, I insist!
